# Introduction

## Samaras and their potential use in biomimetics
*Samaras* (figure \ref{fig:samara_denmark}) are winged autorotating diaspores (dispersal units) [@fauli_effect_2019]. Examples of these dispersal units can be found in maple species, among other plants.

```{r samara_denmark, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align="left", fig.cap="\\textbf{Photo of a ripe samara found in Denmark,} \\textit{Acer} sp., probably \\textit{A. pseudoplatanus}. Own work"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/introduction/maple_samara.png")
```

The term **biomimetics** is derived from the greek word *biomimesis*: [βίος (bios)]{.class lang="el"}, life, and [μίμησις (mīmēsis)]{.class lang="el"} [@noauthor_biomimetics_2026], imitation, meaning mimicking or imitating biology or living nature or organisms [@bhushan_introduction_2018]. Biomimetics is an interdisciplinary field at the interface of biology and engineering that seeks to address technical challenges through the abstraction, transfer, and application of insights derived from biological systems. The German term *Bionik* (not to be confused with *bionics*, which describes biomimetic electronics or robotics) is a portmanteau from the German words **Bio**logie (biology) and Tech**nik** (engineering).
According to Wikipedia, *bionics* is the application of biological systems in engineering and technology whereas the term *biomimetics* describes chemical reactions in a lab where smaller molecules than the macromolecules found in nature are used while being able to replicate the biochemistry of living organisms.
In this thesis though, the first definition is being used in accordance with \acs{vdi} (\acl{vdi}) [@noauthor_bionik_nodate].

When looking at samaras flying or rather falling while autorotating thus slowing down the fall, one can easily come to the conclusion humankind can learn from these objects. Potential use cases are substitutes for parachutes, differently designed rotor blades for \acs{eg} helicopters, or a way to safely land sensor packages on the surface of the planet Mars. The latter is the reason for this bachelor thesis.\

Figure \ref{fig:Ezra_et_al__tipuana_tipu} shows what samaras consist of, using *Tipuana tipu* (not a species of maple) as an example.\

There has already been done a lot of work on this. Liu et al designed an abstracted rectangular artificial samara, which they call *maple-seed-inspired (MSI) rotochute*, claiming it had better efficacy than a natural maple seed (figure \ref{fig:Liu_et_al__msi_rotochute}). The maple samara's leading edge was replaced by a counterweight, the seed (or *root* as seen in figure \ref{fig:Liu_et_al__msi_rotochute}) by the *payload*.

## Leading-edge vortex (LEV)

Samara-bearing trees and shrubs depend on wind to succesfully disperse their seeds (*anemochory*). Samaras generate an unusually high lift that can be explained by the autorotation resulting in a \ac{lev} [@lentink_leading-edge_2009] and thus a reduced rate of descent, giving the samara more air time to be affected by the wind and reaching higher dispersal distances. The \acs{lev} is most prominent near the base of the samara, where the seed is located, at around 25% span, and merges with another vortex formed by the tip of the wing [@lentink_leading-edge_2009]. 

## Native maple species in Germany

Three maple species (figure \ref{fig:leaves_maple_species}) of the family Sapindaceae are considered to be native in Germany: *\acs{A} campestre* (\acs{engl} field maple, \acs{ger} Feld-Ahorn), *\acs{A} platanoides* (\acs{engl} Norway maple, \acs{ger} Spitz-Ahorn) and *\acs{A} pseudoplatanus* (\acs{engl} sycamore, \acs{ger} Berg-Ahorn) [@schmeil_flora_2024; @roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

```{r leaves_maple_species, echo=FALSE, out.width="30%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="\\textbf{Leaves of native maple species in Germany.} (A) \\textit{A. campestre}, (B) \\textit{A. platanoides}, (C) \\textit{A. pseudoplatanus}."}
knitr::include_graphics(
  c("img/introduction/leaf_a_campestre.png",
    "img/introduction/leaf_a_platanoides.png",
    "img/introduction/leaf_a_pseudoplatanus.png")
)
```
\vspace{-2em}Images modified from: [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]

All *Acer* fruits are schizocarp: when ripe, the individual carpels separate along their sutures and break down into single-seeded, nut-like, winged mericarps  [@schmeil_flora_2024] - the two (or, less commonly, three) samaras.
All three maple species in this study are *incompletely monoecious*; the flowers are hermaphroditic or functionally unisexual, while rudiments of the opposite sex are usually present [@schmeil_flora_2024].

Roloff et al. provide a detailed, in-depth description of the three maple species, among other trees. Here is an excerpt of the most valuable information for this thesis.

### *\acs{A} campestre* (field maple)
*\acs{A} campestre* occurs in dry to moist deciduous forests, riparian forests, and shrublands [@schmeil_flora_2024]. It presents as shrub or tree, blossoms in May, is 2-15 (sometimes up to 20) m high [@schmeil_flora_2024]. It can live to be between 150 and 200 years old, flowers start to develop at an age of about 25 years [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. 

Samaras ripen in late September/early October, get to be about 2.5 cm long,  face each other horizontally, and are usually covered with downy hairs, but are sometimes hairless [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

With 5,500 seeds per kilogram, the seed weight falls between that of *\acs{A} platanoides* and *\acs{A} pseudoplatanus* [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].
The fruits therefore have a thousand-grain weight of about 182 g.

### *\acs{A} platanoides* (Norway maple)
*\acs{A} platanoides* occurs in mixed deciduous forests, but in some areas it is only naturalized and is commonly used as park or street tree [@schmeil_flora_2024]. It presents as tree, blossoms April to May, usually grows up to 20 (sometimes up to 35) m high [@schmeil_flora_2024], and gets to live for about 180 years [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. When growing in open areas, *\acs{A} platanoides* reaches sexual maturity as early as 10 to 15 years, but not until 25 to 30 years when growing in a stand [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

*\acs{A} platanoides* bears fruit abundantly almost every year and the samaras ripen in fall [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. They get to be about 5 cm long, hang down in pairs (sometimes in groups of three or more), and the upper edges of the two wings form an obtuse angle, which is a distinguishing feature from *\acs{A} campestre* (horizontal) and *\acs{A} pseudoplatanus* (acute angle) [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

The fruits have a thousand-grain weight (without wings) of 120 to 150 g [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

### *\acs{A} pseudoplatanus* (sycamore)
*\acs{A} pseudoplatanus* occurs in gorge forests and mountain forests, but in some areas it is only naturalized and is used as forest, park, or street tree [@schmeil_flora_2024]. It presents as tree, blossoms April to May, usually up to 25 (sometimes up to 30) m high [@schmeil_flora_2024].
In lowland areas, it can live to be between 150 years old, and 400-500 (up to 600) years in mountain areas, flowers start to develop at an age of about 30 years [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. 

The inflorescence is racemose with 40.000–170.000 fruits per 40 year old tree [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. The samara's wings get to be 3-6 cm long and have a usually distinctly rounded trailing edge [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014]. The samaras are always connected in pairs on the tree, forming an acute to right angle with each other [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

The fruits have a thousand-grain weight of 800 g, the average fruit weight is 128 mg and consists of 63% embryo, 22% pericarp, and 14% wing [@roloff_enzyklopaholzgewachse_2014].

Prof. Dr. Claus Mattheck, \ac{kit}, found out that shapes of a significant number of biological structures and other structures found in nature (figure \ref{fig:mattheck_tensile_triangles}) can be described using so-called **tensile triangles**:\

\begin{quote}
\enquote{The tensile triangles curve appears to be a general design rule in nature with yet unknown limitations and potential.} 
\end{quote}
\hfill [&ndash; [@mattheck_pauli_2018]]{style="float:right"}\

Shapes following the tensile triangles curve have shown to reduce stress in notches [@mattheck_pauli_2018] and allow for efficient use of \enquote{building material} (\acs{eg} wood), and thereby confirming nature's optimzed architecture through evolution.\

### Uniaxial loading

In short, the method for uniaxial loading is as follows: an isosceles right triangle (figure \ref{fig:tensile_triangles_tree}, points EGF) is drawn at the base, \acs{eg} at the intercept of trunk and ground level. Using corner point G and center of the hypotenuse H, a second isosceles triangle is drawn. Repeating with corner point I and center point J, a third and final triangle is drawn.
The method is further explained in [Methods and Materials](#methods-and-materials).

## Motivation: space exploration / landing technologies on Mars and other bodies

By simulating autorotational descend on multiple celestial bodies, Riegler et al came to the conclusion that \enquote{autorotation is not well suited to land large payloads on [Mars]} [@riegler_comparison_2025]. The simulation used vehicle parameters of 1000kg and a 4 rotor blade design. Experiments done in a drop tower at [\acs{zarm}](https://www.zarm.uni-bremen.de/en/) (\acl{zarm}) showed that samaras get into stable autoration in a Mars-like atmosphere (to be published).

**Body**          **Mass** [$kg$]   **Diameter** [$km$]   **Gravity** [$m/s^2$]
---------  ----------------------  --------------------  ----------------------
Earth        $5.97 \cdot 10^{24}$                12,756                     9.8
Mars        $0.642 \cdot 10^{24}$                  6792                     3.7
Venus        $4.87 \cdot 10^{24}$                12,104                     8.9
Titan$^1$   $0.135 \cdot 10^{24}$               5,149.4                     1.4
      
: Celestial body parameters [@noauthor_planetary_nodate]; [1] [@riegler_comparison_2025].  {#tab:planetary_parameters .class key="value"}

Table \ref{tab:planetary_parameters} compares planetary (and other celestial body) parameters, \ref{fig:atmospheric_density_comparison} compares atmospheric density among planets and Titan. These parameters greatly impact samara behavior.

This thesis aims to improve artificial samara design and thereby suggesting design parameters for novel experiments on landing technologies, mainly for Mars exploration.

# Methods and materials

## Samples

More than 200 mostly intact samaras of native maple species were gathered (\>50 per species/location), defective samaras have been discarded so that at least 50 intact samples could be used. The sample's species were identified based on the shape of the leaves (figures \ref{fig:leaves_maple_species}, \ref{fig:maple_leaves_schmeil}), cross-referenced with the samara topology (figure!!) of the closest tree, and it was made sure that no other species of maple were near the gathering site. The four species and locations were as follows:

1.  *Acer campestre* \acs{l}- Loki Schmidt Garten, Hamburg - what3words: [///kennels.slippery.hears](https://w3w.co/kennels.slippery.hears)
2.  *Acer pseudoplatanus* \acs{l}- Stadtpark, Hamburg - what3words: [///engaging.survey.spout](https://w3w.co/engaging.survey.spout)
3.  *Acer platanoides* \acs{l}- Spannskamp, Hamburg - what3words: [///bristle.ruins.curated](https://w3w.co/bristle.ruins.curated)
4.  *Acer platanoides* \acs{l}- IPM, Hamburg - what3words: [///gardens.rattled.yappy](https://w3w.co/gardens.rattled.yappy)

The web service what3words was used as an easy way to keep track of locations.
All samples were gathered between June 22nd and June 28th 2026.

```{r maple_leaves_schmeil, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="\\textbf{Leaves of native maple species in Germany.} (A) \\textit{A. campestre}, (B) \\textit{A. platanoides}, (C) \\textit{A. pseudoplatanus}."}

## Photos for measuring and geometry experiments

An A3 sheet of millimeter paper was placed on the ground and secured with transparent sticky tape. A 10x4 cm cutout of white printer paper was taped on it. One samara at a time was placed on that paper and a sticky note with date/time and species name was placed below.\
A digital camera (Panasonic Lumix G, Model No. DC-FZ100002) was secured on a tripod stand at maximum height, pointed down and leveled via spirit level. Distance from ground to camera lens was measured 134cm. The following settings were chosen to take photos: Focal length 400, S 4, F 11, ISO 125; manual mode. Photos of the setup were taken, see figure \ref{fig:camera_setup}.

50 photos for *Acer pseudoplatanus* and *\acs{A} campestre* and 100 photos for *\acs{A} platanoides* (50 for each of the two samples) were taken by remote control with the Panasonic Image App. The photos were copied to a Laptop and backed up to cloud storage and an external SSD.

## Measuring samaras in FIJI

After opening a photo of a samara in FIJI, four centimeteres were marked using the millimeter sheet (figure \ref{fig:P1116384}). The scale was then set via *Set Scale...* which autofilled the marked pixels. The output was recorded in the macro that was used to measure all the samples, as shown below:
\begin{verbatim}
// Set Scale
run("Set Scale...", "distance=1457.0124 known=4 unit=cm");
\end{verbatim}

```{r}
px_per_mm <- 1457.0124/40
mm_per_px <- 40/1457.0124
```


```{r P1116384, echo=FALSE, out.width="50%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="\\textbf{Photo of a sample of \\textit{A. pseudoplatanus}.} Source: own work"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/fiji/P1116384.JPG")
```

A FIJI macro was written and used to automatically measure the samara's dimensions. The macro first converted the image to a mask with a set threshold of `0,140`, then cropped, then started a particle analysis in which the biggest length of the largest found area was measured. After that the greatest width perpendicular to that length was measured. Lines were drawn onto the mask and results written into the top left corner of the image (figure \ref{fig:P1116384_processed}) as well as written into a CSV (comma-separated values) file.

```{r P1116384_processed, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="\\textbf{Sample of \\textit{A. pseudoplatanus} after processing with FIJI macro.} Source: own work"}
knitr::include_graphics("img/fiji/P1116384_processed.jpg")
```

The results were processed in R code in a `.Rmd` file in RStudio by Posit Software. Mean, standard deviation, standard error and variance were calculated for all samples and for each species/sample separately. Length/width ratios were calculated and tests (Shapiro-Wilk, Levene, ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis) performed.

### Bézier curves

The first Bézier curve experiments were done in Geogebra (figure \ref{fig:geogebra_bezier}; [geogebra.org](https://www.geogebra.org/)). Since this web service can't handle large images and downscales them, cropped sections were used. As the sections were not the same size, Geogebra treated them differently. Therefore the results were not comparable. \par
\indent From then on, Affinity suite ([affinity.studio](https://www.affinity.studio/)) was used for all measurements. Cubic Beziér curves were drawn manually with the Pen tool and fitted to the shape of the samara's trailing edge and leading edge respectively with the Node tool (figure \ref{fig:bezier_pseudoplatanus_affinity}). The curve was exported as SVG and all SVG files handled by a custom Python script, resulting in a machine-readable CSV file, that was imported by R code.

## Stained sections

### Shapiro-Wilk test

H0: sample comes from a normally distributed population.
HA: no normal distribution.

```{r}
shapiro_Acampestre <- shapiro.test(my_data$ratio[my_data$Species == "Acer campestre"])

shapiro_Aplatanoides_IPM <- shapiro.test(my_data$ratio[my_data$Species == "Acer platanoides" & my_data$Location == "IPM"])

shapiro_Aplatanoides_Spannskamp <- shapiro.test(my_data$ratio[my_data$Species == "Acer platanoides" & my_data$Location == "Spannskamp"])

shapiro_Apseudoplatanus <- shapiro.test(my_data$ratio[my_data$Species == "Acer pseudoplatanus"])

shapiro_table <- data.frame(
  Sample = c("Acer campestre", "Acer platanoides (IPM)", "Acer platanoides (Spannskamp)", "Acer pseudoplatanus"),
  Statistic = c(shapiro_Acampestre$statistic, shapiro_Aplatanoides_IPM$statistic, shapiro_Aplatanoides_Spannskamp$statistic, shapiro_Apseudoplatanus$statistic),
  p = c(shapiro_Acampestre$p.value, shapiro_Aplatanoides_IPM$p.value, shapiro_Aplatanoides_Spannskamp$p.value, shapiro_Apseudoplatanus$p.value),
  normality = c("no, p < 0.001","no, p < 0.01", "yes, p > 0.5", "no, p < 0.01")
)

kable(shapiro_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "Results of Shapiro-Wilk tests",
  label = "shapiro") |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

### Levene test

H0: homogeneity of variance.
HA: at least one group with variance unequal to others.

```{r}
my_data$sample <- as.factor(my_data$sample)
levene_results <- car::leveneTest(ratio ~ sample, my_data)

#levene_table <- data.frame(
#  c("Df", "F value", "Pr(>F)")
#)
kable(
  levene_results,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Levene test results",
  label = "levene"
) |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

### ANOVA

Ratio \~ sample

```{r}
mod <- aov(formula = my_data$ratio ~ my_data$sample, data = my_data)

#summary(mod)

anova_tab <- summary(mod)[[1]]
anova_tab$`Pr(>F)` <- format.pval(anova_tab$`Pr(>F)`, digits = 4, na.form="")
kable(anova_tab,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  caption = "ANOVA results",
  label = "anova") |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

Table \ref{tab:anova} shows Anova results.

### Kruskal-Wallis test

```{r}
kruskal <- kruskal.test(ratio ~ sample, data = my_data)

kruskal_table <- data.frame(
  Method = kruskal$method,
  Statistic = unname(kruskal$statistic),
  Degrees_of_Freedom = unname(kruskal$parameter),
  P_value = format.pval(kruskal$p.value, digits = 4)
)

kable(kruskal_table,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Kruskal-Wallis test",
  label = "kruskal") |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

* p-value $< 0.05$: Evidence of a statistically significant difference between at least two groups.
* p-value $\geq 0.05$: Insufficient evidence to conclude that the groups differ.

## Topology Optimization after Mattheck

## Bézier curves

### Trailing Edge

Figures \ref{fig:bezier_pseudoplatanus_affinity} and \ref{fig:geogebra_bezier} shows that the shapes of all three maple species can be described by Bézier curves.

#### Bézier curve simulation

```{r}
v_linetypes = c(
      "1" = "solid",
      "2" = "dashed",
      "3" = "dotted",
      "4" = "dotdash",
      "5" = "longdash",
      "6" = "twodash"
    )
```

```{r}
library(bezier)
t <- seq(0, 1, length=100)
p <- matrix(c(0.48,6.04, 9.56,13.54, 9.22,-4.65, 25.58,6.54), nrow=4, ncol=2, byrow=TRUE)
bezier_points <- bezier(t=t, p=p)

df_bezier_points <- data.frame(bezier_points)
colnames(df_bezier_points) <- c("X","Y")

colnames(p) <- c("X","Y")
rownames(p) <- c("A","B","C","D")
kable(p, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Control points of first attempt of bezier curve on sample of A. pseudoplatanus", label = "control_points") |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

Formula \ref{bezier_dummy}

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{P}(t) = (1-t)^3
\begin{pmatrix}
`r p["A","X"]`\\`r p["A","Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+3(1-t)^2t
\begin{pmatrix}
`r p["B","X"]`\\`r p["B","Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ 3(1-t)t^2
\begin{pmatrix}
`r p["C","X"]`\\`r p["C","Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ t^3
\begin{pmatrix}
`r p["D","X"]`\\`r p["D","Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
\label{bezier_dummy}\end{equation}
$$

Figure \ref{fig:bezier_curve_simulation}

```{r bezier_curves_transformed, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="Bézier curve simulation with transformed data of three Acer species. Source: own work"}
target_length <- 100

mean_angle <- atan2(
  D_global$Y_D - A_global$Y_A,
  D_global$X_D - A_global$X_A
)

mean_length <- sqrt(
  (D_global$X_D - A_global$X_A)^2 +
  (D_global$Y_D - A_global$Y_A)^2
)

data_curve_points_transformed <- data_curve_points_adjusted |> 
  group_by(FileName.x) |> 
  mutate(
    X_A = A_global$X_A,
    Y_A = A_global$Y_A,
    
    X_D = X[Point == "D"][1],
    Y_D = Y[Point == "D"][1],
    
    AD_X = X_D - X_A,
    AD_Y = Y_D - Y_A,
    
    angle_D = atan2(AD_Y, AD_X),
    rotation = mean_angle - angle_D,
    
    length_D = sqrt(AD_X^2 + AD_Y^2),
    
    X_rel = X - X_A,
    Y_rel = Y - Y_A,
    
    X_rot = X_rel * cos(rotation) - Y_rel * sin(rotation),
    Y_rot = X_rel * sin(rotation) + Y_rel * cos(rotation),
    
    X = X_rot * mean_length / length_D + X_A,
    Y = Y_rot * mean_length / length_D + Y_A
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(
    -X_A, -Y_A,
    -X_D, -Y_D,
    -AD_X, -AD_Y,
    -angle_D, -rotation,
    -length_D,
    -X_rel, -Y_rel,
    -X_rot, -Y_rot
  )

bezier_df_transformed <- data_curve_points_transformed |> 
  group_by(FileName.x, Species) |> 
  group_modify(~ {

    # Kontrollpunkte A, B, C, D
    # Jede Zeile = ein Kontrollpunkt
    control_points <- as.matrix(.x[, c("X", "Y")])

    # Parameter t
    t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)

    # Kubische Bézier-Kurve aus 4 Kontrollpunkten
    curve <- bezier(
      t = t,
      p = control_points
    )

    # Als Dataframe zurückgeben
    data.frame(
      t = t,
      X = curve[, 1],
      Y = curve[, 2]
    )
  }) |> 
  ungroup()

bezier_df_transformed <- bezier_df_transformed %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  mutate(
    Sample = dense_rank(FileName.x)
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Kurven plotten
bezier_df_transformed |> group_by(Species) |> mutate(
  n = n_distinct(FileName.x),
  label = paste0(Species,'\nn = ',n)
) |> ggplot(aes(x = X, y = Y, group = FileName.x, color = label, linetype = factor(Sample))) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom') +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = v_linetypes
  )
```

```{r bezier_curves_transformed_with_lines, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="Horizontal lines with mean amplitudes (dotted), vertical lines with mean x values of amplitudes (dashed). Source: own work"}

bezier_extrema <- bezier_df_transformed |>
  group_by(FileName.x) |>
  arrange(X) |>
  mutate(
    slope = c(NA, diff(Y) / diff(X)),
    slope_change = c(NA, diff(sign(slope)))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    # oberes Extremum: Steigung wechselt von + nach -
    X_upper = X[which(slope_change < 0)[1] + 1],
    Y_upper = Y[which(slope_change < 0)[1] + 1],

    # unteres Extremum: Steigung wechselt von - nach +
    X_lower = X[which(slope_change > 0)[1] + 1],
    Y_lower = Y[which(slope_change > 0)[1] + 1]
  )

mean_lower_X <- mean(bezier_extrema$X_lower, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_lower_Y <- mean(bezier_extrema$Y_lower, na.rm = TRUE)

mean_upper_X <- mean(bezier_extrema$X_upper, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_upper_Y <- mean(bezier_extrema$Y_upper, na.rm = TRUE)

vlines = c(mean_lower_X,mean_upper_X)
hlines = c(mean_lower_Y,mean_upper_Y)

# Kurven plotten
bezier_df_transformed |> group_by(Species) |> mutate(
  n = n_distinct(FileName.x),
  label = paste0(Species,'\nn = ',n)
) |> ggplot(aes(x = X, y = Y, group = FileName.x, color = label, linetype = factor(Sample))) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = vlines, color = "#666", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = hlines, color = "#666", linetype = "dotted") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = 'bottom') +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = v_linetypes
  )

```{r bezier_mean_curve, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%", fig.align = "center", fig.show='hold', fig.cap="Mean curve (red) calculated by means of control points of transformed data. Source: own work"}
mean_curve_points <- data_curve_points_transformed |> 
  group_by(Point) |>
  summarise(
    X = mean(X, na.rm = TRUE),
    Y = mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) 

mean_curve <- mean_curve_points |> group_modify(~ {

    # Kontrollpunkte A, B, C, D
    # Jede Zeile = ein Kontrollpunkt
    control_points <- as.matrix(.x[, c("X", "Y")])

    # Parameter t
    t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)

    # Kubische Bézier-Kurve aus 4 Kontrollpunkten
    curve <- bezier(
      t = t,
      p = control_points
    )

    # Als Dataframe zurückgeben
    data.frame(

#### Variance of amplitudes

Variance of maxima: `r var(bezier_extrema$Y_upper)`

Variance of minima: `r var(bezier_extrema$Y_lower)`

#### Distances of mean amplitudes

Horizontal distance between mean amplitudes: `r mean_upper_X - mean_lower_Y`

Vertical distance between mean amplitudes: `r mean_upper_Y - mean_lower_Y`

#### Bézier forumula

Formula \ref{basic_bezier}

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{P}(t)=(1-t)^3A+3(1-t)^2tB+3(1-t)t^2C+t^3D,
\qquad 0\leq t\leq1.\label{basic_bezier}\end{equation}
$$

```{r}
kable(mean_curve_points, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Control points of mean bezier curve", label = "mean_curve_points") |> kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")
```

```{r}
v <- c(
  setNames(round(mean_curve_points$X, 3), paste0(mean_curve_points$Point, "_X")),
  setNames(round(mean_curve_points$Y, 3), paste0(mean_curve_points$Point, "_Y"))
)
```

Put into a Bézier formula (Formula \ref{mean_bezier}):

$$
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{P}(t) = (1-t)^3
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["A_X"]`\\`r v["A_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+3(1-t)^2t
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["B_X"]`\\`r v["B_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ 3(1-t)t^2
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["C_X"]`\\`r v["C_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ t^3
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["D_X"]`\\`r v["D_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
\label{mean_bezier}
\end{equation}
$$
Because $A=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}$, it can be omitted:

$$
\begin{align}
\mathbf{P}(t) = 3(1-t)^2t
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["B_X"]`\\`r v["B_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ 3(1-t)t^2
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["C_X"]`\\`r v["C_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
+ t^3
\begin{pmatrix}
`r v["D_X"]`\\`r v["D_Y"]`
\end{pmatrix}
\label{mean_bezier_Aomitted}
\end{align}
$$

Or in two terms:

$$
\begin{align}
x(t)&=3(1-t)^2t(`r v["B_X"]`)+3(1-t)t^2(`r v["C_X"]`)+`r v["D_X"]`t^3 \\
y(t)&=3(1-t)^2t(`r v["B_Y"]`)+3(1-t)t^2(`r v["C_Y"]`)
\label{mean_bezier_xy}
\end{align}
$$

# Globalen Mittelpunkt aller ursprünglichen A-Punkte berechnen
A_global_le <- data_curve_points_le_merged |> 
  filter(Point == "A") |> 
  summarise(
    X_A = mean(X, na.rm = TRUE),
    Y_A = mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

D_global_le <- data_curve_points_le_merged |> 
  filter(Point == "D") |> 
  summarise(
    X_D = mean(X, na.rm = TRUE),
    Y_D = mean(Y, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# Für jede Kurve den individuellen A-Punkt bestimmen
data_curve_points_le_adjusted <- data_curve_points_le_merged |> 
  group_by(FileName.x) |> 
  mutate(
    X_A_original = X[Point == "A"][1],
    Y_A_original = Y[Point == "A"][1],
    
    X = X - X_A_original + A_global_le$X_A,
    Y = Y - Y_A_original + A_global_le$Y_A
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(-X_A_original, -Y_A_original)

bezier_df_le <- data_curve_points_le_adjusted |> 
  group_by(FileName.x, Species) |> 
  group_modify(~ {

    # Kontrollpunkte A, B, C, D
    # Jede Zeile = ein Kontrollpunkt
    control_points <- as.matrix(.x[, c("X", "Y")])

    # Parameter t
    t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)

    # Kubische Bézier-Kurve aus 4 Kontrollpunkten
    curve <- bezier(
      t = t,
      p = control_points
    )

    # Als Dataframe zurückgeben
    data.frame(
      t = t,
      X = curve[, 1],
      Y = curve[, 2]
    )
  }) |> 
  ungroup()

bezier_df_le <- bezier_df_le |> 
  group_by(Species) |> 
  mutate(
    Sample = dense_rank(FileName.x)
  ) |> 
  ungroup()

# Kurven plotten
plot_bezier_df_le <- bezier_df_le |> group_by(Species) |> mutate(
  n = n_distinct(FileName.x),
  label = paste0(Species,'\nn = ',n)
) |> ggplot(aes(x = X, y = Y, group = FileName.x, color = label, linetype = factor(Sample))) +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.5, alpha = 0.5) +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = 'none') +
  guides(linetype = "none") +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = v_linetypes
  )

mean_angle_le <- atan2(
  D_global_le$Y_D - A_global_le$Y_A,
  D_global_le$X_D - A_global_le$X_A
)

mean_length_le <- sqrt(
  (D_global_le$X_D - A_global_le$X_A)^2 +
  (D_global_le$Y_D - A_global_le$Y_A)^2
)

data_curve_points_le_transformed <- data_curve_points_le_adjusted |> 
  group_by(FileName.x) |> 
  mutate(
    X_A = A_global_le$X_A,
    Y_A = A_global_le$Y_A,
    
    X_D = X[Point == "D"][1],
    Y_D = Y[Point == "D"][1],
    
    AD_X = X_D - X_A,
    AD_Y = Y_D - Y_A,
    
    angle_D = atan2(AD_Y, AD_X),
    rotation = mean_angle_le - angle_D,
    
    length_D = sqrt(AD_X^2 + AD_Y^2),
    
    X_rel = X - X_A,
    Y_rel = Y - Y_A,
    
    X_rot = X_rel * cos(rotation) - Y_rel * sin(rotation),
    Y_rot = X_rel * sin(rotation) + Y_rel * cos(rotation),
    
    X = X_rot * mean_length_le / length_D + X_A,
    Y = Y_rot * mean_length_le / length_D + Y_A
  ) |> 
  ungroup() |> 
  select(
    -X_A, -Y_A,
    -X_D, -Y_D,
    -AD_X, -AD_Y,
    -angle_D, -rotation,
    -length_D,
    -X_rel, -Y_rel,
    -X_rot, -Y_rot
  )

bezier_df_le_transformed <- data_curve_points_le_transformed |> 
  group_by(FileName.x, Species) |> 
  group_modify(~ {

    # Kontrollpunkte A, B, C, D
    # Jede Zeile = ein Kontrollpunkt
    control_points <- as.matrix(.x[, c("X", "Y")])

    # Parameter t
    t <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 100)

    # Kubische Bézier-Kurve aus 4 Kontrollpunkten
    curve <- bezier(
      t = t,
      p = control_points
    )

    # Als Dataframe zurückgeben
    data.frame(
      t = t,
      X = curve[, 1],
      Y = curve[, 2]
    )
  }) |> 
  ungroup()

    Sample = dense_rank(FileName.x)

bezier_extrema_le <- bezier_df_le_transformed |>
  group_by(FileName.x) |>
  arrange(X) |>
  mutate(
    slope = c(NA, diff(Y) / diff(X)),
    slope_change = c(NA, diff(sign(slope)))
  ) |>
  summarise(
    # oberes Extremum: Steigung wechselt von + nach -
    X_upper = X[which(slope_change < 0)[1] + 1],
    Y_upper = Y[which(slope_change < 0)[1] + 1],

    # unteres Extremum: Steigung wechselt von - nach +
    X_lower = X[which(slope_change > 0)[1] + 1],
    Y_lower = Y[which(slope_change > 0)[1] + 1]
  )

mean_lower_X_le <- mean(bezier_extrema_le$X_lower, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_lower_Y_le <- mean(bezier_extrema_le$Y_lower, na.rm = TRUE)

mean_upper_X_le <- mean(bezier_extrema_le$X_upper, na.rm = TRUE)
mean_upper_Y_le <- mean(bezier_extrema_le$Y_upper, na.rm = TRUE)

vlines_le = c(mean_lower_X_le,mean_upper_X_le)
hlines_le = c(mean_lower_Y_le,mean_upper_Y_le)

  Y = approx(x = mean_curve_le$X, y = mean_curve_le$Y, xout = mean_upper_X)$y
)
target_lower <- data.frame(
  X = mean_lower_X,
  Y = approx(x = mean_curve_le$X, y = mean_curve_le$Y, xout = mean_lower_X)$y
)
label_upper <- paste(round((target_upper$Y-mean_upper_Y)/px_per_mm, 1), " mm")
label_lower <- paste(round((target_lower$Y-mean_lower_Y)/px_per_mm, 1), " mm")

plot_bezier_df_mean_curves +
  annotate("point", x = mean_upper_X, y = mean_upper_Y) + 
  annotate("point", x = mean_lower_X, y = mean_lower_Y) +
  
  annotate("point", x = target_upper$X, y = target_upper$Y) +
  annotate("point", x = target_lower$X, y = target_lower$Y) +
  
  geom_segment(aes(x = mean_upper_X, y = mean_upper_Y, xend = target_upper$X, yend = target_upper$Y), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = mean_lower_X, y = mean_lower_Y, xend = target_lower$X, yend = target_lower$Y), alpha = 0.5) +
  
  annotate("text", x = mean_upper_X, y = (target_upper$Y+mean_upper_Y)/2, label = label_upper) +
  annotate("text", x = mean_lower_X, y = (target_lower$Y+mean_lower_Y)/2, label = label_lower)
  
```


# Discussion

Probleme: 

- beim Messen: Übergang zwischen Same und Flügel nicht immer gleich. Mal klar abgegrenzt, mal mit fließendem Übergang; Lösung: ganze Frucht ausmessen
- Auslösen an der Kamera führt zu verwackeltem Bild, Remote Control App löst das Problem. (Verzögerung auch Option, aber Zeitverlust.)
- Stichprobe mit 50 Früchten pro Spezies groß genug, besser wären unabhängiere Daten. Z.B. 5 Bäume pro Spezies, jeweils 10 Früchte aus verschiedenen Blütenständen.

- Since Geogebra can't handle large images and downscales them, screenshots were taken and experiments done on them. As the screenshots were not the same size, Geogebra treated them differently. From then on, Affinity suite was used for all measurements. Cubic Beziér curves were drawn manually with the Pen tool and fitted to the shape of the samara's trailing edge and leading edge respectively with the Node tool. The curve was exported as SVG and all SVG files handled by a custom Python script, resulting in a machine-readable CSV file, that was imported by R.

- ties in Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, so Shapiro-Wilk test was used

- nur eine Stichprobe normalverteilt

- keine Varianzhomogenität

- ANOVA nicht aussagekräftig, trotzdem gemacht

- erneut: bessere Stichproben für weitere Untersuchungen


# Conclusion

## Dual-use concerns
While this research could support improving artificial samara-like flyers and thereby optimize the deployment and distribution of monitoring stations and sensors, it could in principle be adapted for military applications, \acs{eg} in development of drones or airdropped explosives. This thesis doesn't provide any instructions on construction, and the findings are presented at a level of abstraction intended to limit misuse while preserving scientific value. The residual risk is assessed low, since a slow rate of descent and a  non-self-propelled aircraft are unlikely to be of much use in warfare. The potential benefits outweigh the minor risks mentioned here. 

## Outlook

More research needed:

- better data, multiple trees of same species
- compare to fall velocity / stability
- print artificial samara after these design parameters and compare
